papers.title: Continuous Subcutaneous Foslevodopa/Foscarbidopa Improves Nonmotor Symptoms and Fluctuations in Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Nonmotor fluctuations (NMFs) in Parkinson's disease (PD) represent a heterogeneous and disabling feature often linked to pulsatile dopaminergic stimulation from oral levodopa. Continuous subcutaneous foslevodopa/foscarbidopa infusion (CSFLI) provides 24-h levodopa delivery, with established motor benefits but limited real-world data on NMFs. We investigated changes in motor complications, nonmotor symptoms, and NMFs over 3 months after initiation of CSFLI. METHODS: In this prospective, single-center, real-world study, 66 patients with advanced PD initiated CSFLI. Longitudinal 3-month data were available for 40 patients. Motor complications were assessed with the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) Part IV, motor severity with UPDRS Part III, and nonmotor symptoms with the Nonmotor Symptom Scale (NMSS); nonmotor fluctuations were evaluated with the Nonmotor Fluctuation Assessment questionnaire (NoMoFa). Additional validated scales assessed sleep, mood, fatigue, autonomic, and behavioral symptoms. Longitudinal changes were analyzed using paired parametric or non-parametric tests, as appropriate, with FDR correction. RESULTS: After 3 months, motor complications significantly improved, with reductions in OFF time and ON time with dyskinesias. Nonmotor symptom burden also improved, with significant reductions in NoMoFa total and NMF-OFF scores, whereas NMF-ON remained unchanged. Improvements were also observed in sleep-related symptoms, depressive symptoms, and quality of life, whereas apathy, autonomic symptoms, and daytime sleepiness did not significantly change. CONCLUSIONS: CSFLI was associated with improvements in motor complications and nonmotor fluctuations, particularly OFF-related NMFs, together with benefits in specific nonmotor symptoms. These findings provide preliminary real-world evidence supporting a potential role of CSFLI in the management of NMFs in PD.

papers.title: Identification and experimental validation of candidate biomarkers for Parkinson's Disease through integrated bioinformatics, Mendelian randomization, and machine learning.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Identifying reliable biomarkers and therapeutic targets is important for improving the early diagnosis and treatment of Parkinson's disease (PD). This study aimed to identify PD-related core genes, validate their expression, and explore potential therapeutic drugs. METHODS: PD transcriptomic datasets were analyzed using differential expression analysis, Mendelian randomization, and machine learning. Candidate genes were validated using quantitative PCR (qPCR) in an MPTP-induced PD mouse model. Potential drugs were screened using the DSigDB database, followed by molecular docking and 100-ns molecular dynamics simulations to evaluate protein-ligand binding and stability. RESULTS: Seven potential core genes-AMIGO2, ATG7, CDK2AP2, CYP27A1, MT1X, NIPSNAP1, and TTC19-were identified. AMIGO2, ATG7, NIPSNAP1, and TTC19 were downregulated, whereas CDK2AP2, CYP27A1, and MT1X were upregulated. The results of animal experiments validated the abnormal expression of ATG7, NIPSNAP1, TTC19, CYP27A1, and MT1X. Drug screening identified 239 candidate compounds, five of which met the screening criteria. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations provided computational support for relatively stable interactions between the top three drug-target complexes. CONCLUSION: This study identified several PD-related core genes and experimentally validated the expression of selected genes in an MPTP-induced PD mouse model. In addition, several potential therapeutic compounds were identified through computational analyses, providing candidates for further experimental investigation.

papers.title: Glymphatic Dysfunction Drives High-Urea-Induced Neurodegeneration in Parkinson's Disease.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Disruption of brain urea homeostasis has been implicated in neurodegenerative disorders, yet its molecular mechanisms remain elusive. This study aimed to investigate how urea metabolic disturbance drives neurodegeneration through astrocytic polarity impairment and to identify potential therapeutic targets. METHODS: A high-urea mouse model was generated by urea transporter B (UT-B) knockout. Pharmacological inhibition and genetic intervention were applied to examine dipeptidyl peptidase-like protein 6 (DPP6), protein kinase C eta (PKCη), and aquaporin-4 (AQP4) expression and localization in astrocytes. Glymphatic clearance, α-synuclein (α-syn) pathology propagation, and dopaminergic neurodegeneration were evaluated. RESULTS: Urea upregulated astrocytic DPP6, activated PKCη signaling, and induced AQP4 endocytosis with loss of membrane polarity, leading to impaired glymphatic clearance, accelerated α-syn spread, and dopaminergic neuronal degeneration. Mechanistically, the DPP6-PKCη axis directly regulated AQP4 membrane localization; inhibiting this pathway pharmacologically or genetically rescued all pathological phenotypes. CONCLUSIONS: This study reveals that urea metabolic disruption promotes neurodegenerative progression via the DPP6-PKCη-AQP4 pathway by compromising astrocytic polarity, offering new therapeutic targets for Parkinson's disease. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

papers.title: Improving the clinical trial landscape for Parkinson syndromes in Germany.
papers.abstract: Germany has a longstanding tradition of excellence in neuroscience and Parkinson's research, supported by outstanding academic institutions, specialized clinical centers, and a strong scientific community. Building on this strong foundation, the country now has the opportunity to transform its clinical research landscape into a more integrated ecosystem for Parkinson syndromes. Despite major advances in molecular understanding, biomarker development, and therapeutic innovation, important structural, regulatory, financial, and organizational barriers continue to limit the full translational potential of German Parkinson research. Participants in an expert workshop identified identify recurring challenges, including fragmented trial infrastructures, slow and bureaucratic regulatory procedures, insufficient funding for investigator-initiated clinical research, limited integration of patient organizations, and suboptimal patient recruitment pathways. This workshop-derived perspective outlines a strategic framework to elevate Germany from a country with excellent individual centers to a globally competitive and integrated hub for innovative Parkinson clinical research. Key recommendations include transforming the German Parkinson Study Group into a nationally coordinated, service-oriented trial network; establishing centralized digital and regulatory infrastructures; diversifying public and philanthropic funding; implementing platform and observational trial structures; strengthening incentives for participating centers; and enhancing patient engagement through national registries, decentralized trial approaches, real-world data based evidence surveillance, and systematic integration of patient organizations. The authors argue that Germany must move beyond isolated university-based structures toward a nationally coordinated and highly efficient research ecosystem capable of rapidly delivering disease-modifying and precision medicine trials. papers.title: Spatiotemporally resolved single-nucleus transcriptomics reveals cellular and regional vulnerability in the midbrain in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is clinically and biologically heterogeneous, and ethnic differences may influence its pathogenesis. However, single-nucleus transcriptomic data from East Asian populations remain limited. Here, we present a spatially resolved single-nucleus transcriptomic atlas of the human substantia nigra (SN) across the PD continuum, control, incidental Lewy body disease (iLBD), and advanced PD, in pathologically confirmed Korean individuals. Our integrative analysis revealed early α-synuclein aggregation in the ventrolateral SN, subtype-selective vulnerability of dopaminergic neurons, and relative preservation of the dorsomedial SN and ventral tegmental area. Trajectory and gene regulatory network analyses of astrocytes and microglia revealed spatiotemporally distinct, disease-associated glial responses, each driven by divergent molecular programs. We also identified two transcriptionally distinct vascular spatial clusters that exhibited differential vulnerability and remodeling. Spatial ligand-receptor analysis of α-synuclein-positive regions revealed intercellular signaling events associated with early pathology, including extracellular matrix remodeling and synaptic adhesion, which were prominent in the iLBD but largely diminished in advanced PD. Integration with PD genome-wide association studies using MAGMA demonstrated differential coupling between genetic risk, spatially resolved cell-state programs, and pseudotime-inferred microglial dynamics across ancestries. This study provides the first high-resolution, spatially mapped single-nucleus transcriptomic resource from an East Asian PD cohort, illuminating early perturbations in the midbrain intercellular and microenvironment that may underlie selective dopaminergic vulnerability and guide the development of ancestry-informed therapeutic strategies.
